newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Corruption probe threatens Israel's Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Corruption probe threatens Israel's Netanyahu.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu, already beset by a breakdown in Middle East peacemaking, faced a potential threat to his government on Tuesday when police completed a 995-page corruption inquiry.

Media buzzed with reports that police had recommended bringing charges against two or three people close to the prime minister. But prosecutors, who will make the decision, ordered the findings be kept under wraps until they decide if to accept the police recommendations.

"The investigation has reached an end after 12 weeks during which 60 depositions were taken," police said. "The prosecution will decide on the nature and timing for bringing the inquiry before the public."

Police have been looking into the ill-fated appointment of an attorney general in January. Israel's Channel One television alleged that a Netanyahu ally on trial had pushed candidate Roni Bar-On for the job in hopes of winning a plea bargain.

Amid a swirl of suspicions Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi, the prime minister's director-general Avigdor Lieberman, and the man on trial, Aryeh Deri of the religious Shas party, have all denied any wrongdoing.
Bar-On himself quit hours after being appointed amid criticism he was professionally unfit for the job.

Netanyahu's Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said on Tuesday he believed prosecutors would reject any recommendations to bring charges, telling Channel Two television: "I believe and hope that the state prosecutor won't adopt them."

Earlier Naveh shrugged off a Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper report that police were struggling over whether to recommend charging Netanyahu, saying: "I am sure and convinced the prime minister's hands are clean."

Whatever the outcome, legal analyst Moshe Negbi said: "This is the most severe affair in the country's history". Two cabinet ministers have been saying for weeks the government must fall if the allegations prove true.

The scandal has cast a giant shadow over Netanyahu's government at a time peace moves are deadlocked over his start of a Jewish settlement and over allegations Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat gave a "green light" to violence and terrorism.
Netanyahu got more bad news from his statistics bureau on Tuesday. March inflation was a higher-than-expected 1.0 percent.

The prime minister has also been battling charges by a leading industrialist that he is a poor manager and a report he has been speaking with one voice to Israelis and another to an outside world critical of his Jewish settlement policy.

Yedioth Ahronoth said this week that Netanyahu, under world pressure over his Jewish settlement policy, had promised Italy's prime minister to delay for three years the controversial building of homes for Jews on a hill in Arab East Jerusalem.
When Netanyahu broke ground on the Har Homa Jewish settlement on March 18, he said he was asserting a right of Jews to live anywhere in the holy city.

But much of the world has criticised Netanyahu, saying he should not try to pre-empt peace deals with Palestinians which leave to talks running until May 1999 the fate of East Jerusalem, an area claimed by both sides.

Netanyahu, locked in a coalition with right-wingers like himself who oppose peace deals requiring him to swap more land for peace with Arabs, has in recent days said he might forge a government with the Labour party he ousted last May.
While opposing the peace deals Netanyahu has said he will honour Israel's international obligations.
